chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Ali ibn Al-Nu'man, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Ala'a the seller of As-Sabiriyyah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a woman who entrusted a man with wealth. When death approached her, she said to him, 'The wealth that I gave to you is for so-and-so woman.' The woman died, and her guardians came to the man and said to him, 'There was wealth for our companion, and we do not see it except with you, so swear to us that there is nothing for us with you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'If she was trusted (reliable) in his presence, let him swear; and if she was suspected (unreliable) in his presence, he should not swear, and he should place the matter upon what it was. Indeed, for her from her wealth is one-third.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a man entrusted with wealth when the deceased woman's guardians claim it, based on her reliability?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between 'ma'munah' (reliable/trustworthy) and 'muttahamah' (suspected/unreliable) status when determining the distribution of entrusted wealth after death. The ruling emphasizes that the guardian's oath is contingent upon the deceased's known reliability; if she was trustworthy, the man swears he owes nothing, but if she was suspected, the burden shifts, and a specific portion (one-third) is allocated to her estate, reflecting a nuanced approach to evidentiary standards in inheritance disputes.

en.hubeali: Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Al Husayn Bin Saeed, from Ali Bin Al Noman, from Abdullah Bin Muskan, from Ala’a Bayaa Al Sabiry who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about a woman who entrusted a man with some wealth. So when the death preseted itself to her, she said to him, ‘The wealth which I had handed it over to you is for so and so woman’. So the woman died, and her guardians came over to the man so they said to him, ‘There used to be some wealth for our companion, but we do not see it except to be with you, therefore swear an oath for us that there is nothing for us with you, anything’. Should he swear for them?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If she (the deceased) was trusted (by her guardians), so let him swear, and if she was an accused (by them) in his presence, so he should not swear, and he should place the matter upon what it used to be. But rather, for her, from her wealth, is a third’.
en.sarwar: 11. Ahmad ibn Muhammad has narrated from al-Husayn ibn Sa‘id from Ali ibn al-Nu’man from ‘Abd Allah ibn Muskan from al-‘Ala’ Bayya’ al-Sabiriy who has narrated the following: “I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a woman who leaves in trust with a man a certain amount of assets; and when the time of her death comes, she tells him that the asset she has left with him belongs to so and so female person.

The woman dies and her people come to him and ask him to take an oath that she has not left anything with him. Must he take an oath in such case? He (the Imam) said, Tf he trusts her he can take an oath but if she is accused, he must not take an oath and instead leave the matter as is; only one-third belongs to her, after all.”’
